pending_items.title: In boost for Netanyahu, judges question corruption trial charges
pending_items.content:
Judges in the long-running corruption trial of Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu handed his defence a major boost on Wednesday in recommending the prosecution drop one of the cases in which he is accused of bribery.

The recommendations, which came as Israel's longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival, were immediately cheered by Netanyahu's right-wing allies who demanded the trial be brought to an end.

Netanyahu's main rival Gadi Eisenkot has been tasked with forming a government after inconclusive October 27 elections and if Netanyahu is no longer prime minister, he would lose his leverage to avoid a potential jail sentence.

During a hearing in Jerusalem regarding three corruption cases against Netanyahu, judges recommended dropping one, reconsidering another and suggested resolving the third through an agreement, Israeli media reported.

In Case 4000, in which Netanyahu is accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, judges indicated there was little chance of a conviction.

That case is considered to be the most serious Netanyahu faces and concerns him allegedly offering regulatory favours for a telecoms company in exchange for favourable media coverage.

Netanyahu is alleged to have negotiated with Shaul Elovitch, the controlling shareholder of Israeli telecommunications giant Bezeq, to get positive coverage on his Walla news site in exchange for policies benefiting Bezeq.

On Wednesday, Israeli media reported Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman as saying that proving the bribery charge in that case faced "considerable difficulties".

Netanyahu, who has been in power on and off for three decades, has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and denounced the cases as a politically motivated plot against him.

He is the first sitting Israeli premier to stand trial.

Israel's Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, who was unusually summoned to the hearing on Wednesday, said she would consider the judges' recommendations and was ready for either a verdict or a plea deal.

In the second case, known as Case 2000, Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust over allegedly negotiating with the owner of the Yediot Aharonot newspaper for favourable media coverage.

In exchange, Netanyahu allegedly raised the possibility of pushing for legislation to limit the circulation of Israel Hayom, a free newspaper that is the main rival to Yediot.

Judges on Wednesday questioned whether his actions amounted to criminal conduct and recommended reconsidering the arguments in the case.

In a third case, Case 1000, Netanyahu faces fraud and breach of trust charges over allegedly receiving luxury gifts including cigars, champagne and jewellery from wealthy individuals in exchange for financial or personal favours.

Judges on Wednesday recommended finding an agreement in that case so it can be brought to a conclusion.

Netanyahu's allies welcomed the court's recommendations.

"After years of persecution against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the time has come to put an end to a trial that was flawed from the outset, that divides Israeli society and is exacting a heavy price from the state," Israel Katz, who is the defence minister in Netanyahu's caretaker government, wrote on X.

Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir said the cases against Netanyahu were "collapsing".

"This is a witch hunt by the deep state, which wants to bring down the right and its leader. We won't let them," he wrote on X.

Netanyahu's corruption trial opened in May 2020.

During his most recent term, which started in late 2022, Netanyahu proposed far-reaching judicial reforms that critics say sought to weaken the courts.

With coalition negotiations underway, Eisenkot's camp is already trying to start unravelling some of the Netanyahu-era judicial reforms in parliament.

US President Donald Trump had pushed Israeli President Isaac Herzog to issue Netanyahu a pardon, with Netanyahu himself submitting a formal request at the end of last year.

pending_items.title: At Turkey’s COP31, artists put fossil fuels in the frame
pending_items.content:
ANTALYA, Turkey — Silver-plated dried plants rotated eerily in their terracotta pots. An old typewriter rose above a hill of shredded paper. There was also a portrait of Enver Pasha, the war minister who led the Ottoman Empire into World War I, by Osman Hamdi Bey, who holds the Turkish auction record with his “Young Woman Reading,” which sold for about $7.8 million in 2019. In an 8,100-square-meter (roughly 2-acre) gallery in the Green Zone of the sprawling COP31 complex in Antalya, COPArt, the summit’s art program, put the ecological angst of artists from Turkey and beyond on display under the title “Still Possible.”

Many negotiators, activists and journalists will remember COP31 for how it ended. Initially scheduled for Nov. 9-20, the summit ran two days over as delegations struggled to reach a deal. It became the first COP since Copenhagen in 2009 to close without a cover decision, the overarching political text known this time as the Antalya Pact. The European Union and dozens of other countries rejected a final draft that made no direct mention of fossil fuels.

For the summit’s cultural organizers, however, the scorecard reads differently. “We did a world first,” Nagihan Ozel, who directed COPArt and curated its contemporary art selection, told the program’s closing panel on Nov. 20. Meanwhile, the Turkish Environment Ministry boasted that the United Nations had recognized COPArt as a legacy of Turkey’s presidency, to be carried forward at future climate summits.

“The work for COPArt started in May,” Samed Karagoz, COPArt’s art director and curator of its Palestinian section, told Al-Monitor. “We organized it in five parts: Ottoman calligraphy, classical Turkish painting, contemporary art, digital art and Palestine.”

“We reached out to galleries in the country and abroad, to private collectors and to artists directly,” Karagoz said. He cited as a major success the loan of Anselm Kiefer’s “Fur Rabbi Low,” in which the German artist uses a pair of scales to weigh what humans can create against what they owe for doing so.

People view art on display at the COPArt gallery in the Green Zone at the COP31 UNFCCC Climate Conference, Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 19, 2026.

Nearby, Eva Jospin’s “Foret” builds a woodland out of cardboard, itself a product of felled trees: Art can remake a forest far more easily than nature can. Clarissa Tossin preserved in silicone a maple tree from Mulhouse, France, that had died from heat and drought, calling the work “Death by Heat Wave.” Turkish artist Vuslat coated dried mullein in silver for “Last Seen,” with each plant sculpture resting on a water-filled clay base inscribed with the year one of five plant species driven to extinction by humans was last seen in the wild.

Fossil fuels, the issue that sank the Antalya Pact, also found their way onto the cultural scene, both inside and outside the official program.

Greenpeace and Danish artist Thomas Dambo, known for his giant trolls built from scrap wood, planted a six-meter (20-feet) Trojan Horse in front of Konyaalti municipality. A trapdoor in its belly spilled plastic waste, which Greenpeace presented as a symbol of an oil and gas industry betting on plastics to sustain its growth. Inside the venue, Greenpeace laid a 3D floor installation titled “Don’t Fall For Fossil Fuels” along a main corridor.

The Polish Institute in Istanbul, inaugurated in August, brought the debate into the Green Zone with a panel titled “From Coal Dust to the Light: Upper Silesia, A European Laboratory for the Energy Transition and Beyond.” Co-organized with the EU Delegation to Turkey, the panel featured speakers including Lukasz Galusek, director of the Silesian Museum in Katowice. The museum transformed a former coal mine into a “culture mine,” with galleries 14 meters (46 meters) underground and the old Warszawa II hoisting shaft now serving as a viewing tower overlooking the city.

“For centuries, Upper Silesia ran on its coal mines,” said Radosław Sadowski, the institute’s director, who moderated the panel. “EU accession changed the direction of our energy policy. Former industrial sites became museums and business hubs through a fair transition that preserved the region’s heritage. It is a lesson worth sharing with other countries, including our host.”

The national canon goes to the coast

The Turkish selection resembled a museum survey, featuring works by late Ottoman and early Republican painters such as Seker Ahmet Pasha, Osman Hamdi Bey, Hoca Ali Riza and Ibrahim Calli. Scattered across different pavilions, “Six Masters, Six Traces” brought together the trailblazers Fahrelnissa Zeid, Burhan Dogancay, Omer Uluc, Devrim Erbil, Mehmet Guleryuz and Haluk Akakce. Some pieces, borrowed from collectors’ homes and offices, went on public display for the first time.

“We also used the opportunity to introduce Ottoman calligraphy to our foreign visitors,” Karagoz said. “Few of them would have seen it elsewhere.”

The most openly political room was the Palestinian section . Some of its works had previously been exhibited at the Mahmoud Darwish Museum in Ramallah, where Karagoz curated an exhibition of Turkish artist Ahmet Yusuf Aygec’s “Posters for the Olive Tree in Exile” in July. The section also featured works by the late Palestinian painter Suleiman Mansour and Nabil Anani.

“The Palestine section was a display of our stance on this issue as the host country,” Karagoz said, adding that COPArt drew an average of 5,000 visitors a day.

The summit also came with a soundtrack. The ministry set the tone on Oct. 23 with its own English-language anthem, “Let's COP.” Pop star Tarkan followed a week before the summit with “Wake Up,” an English-language reworking of his 2008 song “Uyan.” Sertab Erener, Turkey's 2003 Eurovision winner, added “One Home,” a song that Kurum shared on the summit's opening day.

“Let's COP” turned out to be an easy target. Germany's weekly Freitag called it Eurovision-style, noted that COP is not a verb and reported that officials had admitted to using artificial intelligence in its production. The paper contrasted the song with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's announcement, at the start of the summit, of two new oil fields, Gaziler and Cardakli, expected to increase Turkish oil output by 30%.

pending_items.title: Houthis say they attacked Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery in retaliation for deadly strikes
pending_items.content:
Yemen's Houthi movement claimed responsibility for an attack on Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, on Wednesday, describing it as retaliation for repeated Saudi strikes that have killed scores of civilians.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a post on X that the refinery attack caused fires and came in retaliation for the "brutal Saudi aggression against our country, including its targeting of passenger buses and citizens' trucks in the Al-Maqatirah district of Lahij, as well as other crimes in the capital, Sanaa, and the governorates."

The attack in the district of Lahij earlier this week killed at least 26 people.

In a follow-up post on X, Saree responded to Saudi threats to retaliate against Yemen's civilian Hodeidah port, which Saudi Arabia has already bombed, by warning that all "enemy Saudi ports along the Red Sea coast will be targets".

"We warn employees, workers and those near these ports to evacuate them immediately and stay away, and we call on all shipping companies to remove their ships from those ports immediately," the post added.

Ansar Allah, known as the Houthis, which controls the capital Sanaa and much of north and western Yemen, has been firing missiles at Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and office buildings since Yemen's frozen civil war reignited in July in a spillover from the Israeli-US war on Iran .

Riyadh broke the ceasefire, which also included Saudi Arabia, when it bombed Sanaa's international airport on 13 July.

Since then, the Saudi military has struggled to contain the Houthis and their ability to counter Saudi-backed forces in Yemen.

The ongoing attacks are wreaking havoc on the Saudi economy, oil infrastructure and the country's international image.

Airlines have cancelled international flights from the Saudi capital, Riyadh, while previous attacks on the country’s oil infrastructure have disrupted oil supplies.

The attacks have also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including football's AFC Asian Cup and the flagship Future Investment Initiative conference.

Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudis said that air defences had intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura in the country's Eastern Province. They did not deny that the attack had struck the oil refinery there.

Satellite images reviewed by Reuters showed large swathes of thick black smoke around the refinery, covering an area spanning around 600 square kilometres.

The Houthis have previously targeted Ras Tanura, which has a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, during the conflict.

The refinery forms part of a strategic complex on the kingdom's Gulf coast facing Iran, through which the country exported most of its oil before the Israel-US war on Iran started on 28 February.

Since then, Saudi Arabia has had to send some of its oil through Yanbu on the west coast along the Red Sea, which receives oil via the East-West pipeline and has also faced attacks.

Separately, Houthi spokesman Saree had also said the group had attacked Riyadh's financial district in three phases.

Saudi civil defence said a strike on Tuesday wounded 11 people at a tower in Riyadh’s financial district. The tallest building in the capital, the tower houses the headquarters of the Public Investment Fund, the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund. It was the second strike on the tower in less than a week.

The first, on 19 November, damaged the building but caused no injuries. Saudi civil defence posted an image on Tuesday of the landmark tower showing some damage about halfway up the facade, similar to the impact of last week's attack.
